Sponsio

An AI assistant that helps amateur clubs find local sponsors

Final project report
Monetizing Data and AI, MSc 1
November 2026

Team: [name to add], [name to add], [name to add], [name to add]

1. Summary

Amateur sports clubs depend on local sponsors, yet the volunteers who prepare each offer have little time, and they often propose slots that are already sold. Sponsio is an AI assistant that turns the name of a local business into a ready-to-send offer. It proposes only the slots the club has free, avoids sector conflicts with current sponsors, links the offer to the club's declared needs, and shows the sponsor's logo on photo-realistic mock-ups of the club's kit, boards and minibus.

We target mid-size and flagship clubs, about 56,100 in France. The plan is a subscription of €15 a month for mid-size clubs and €150 a month for flagship clubs, which is about 23% and 20% of the value created for them. With 400 clubs after three years, annual recurring revenue reaches €136,800. The business breaks even at 122 clubs in month 11, and we ask for €35,000 to cover 18 months.

The prototype is working and measured: an offer costs about $0.0006 and takes four to five seconds to write. We have no paying client yet. The most fragile assumption is the uplift in sponsoring, which pilots with three clubs will measure. The link to the live demonstration is given in the submission email.

2. The problem

Sponsorship is a modest but important share of a club's resources. A study by the French Olympic Committee estimates that partnerships bring about 9% of the resources of sports associations, and that 37% of clubs run a deficit. Budgets vary widely: 63% of clubs have less than €10,000, while the average mid-size club has €80,145 and the average flagship club €917,857.

Our persona is Julien, the volunteer treasurer of a football club with 320 members. He writes each sponsor pitch alone, in the evening. We believe three problems follow. The pitches are generic, so a bakery and a garage receive the same text. The offers include slots that are already sold, or sectors that conflict with a current sponsor. Nothing connects the offer to what the club needs this season. These three problems are hypotheses taken from the structure of the work, not findings from interviews. The first action of the pilot phase is to test them in ten calls with mid-size clubs.

3. The solution and its moment of truth

The moment of truth is simple: a business name goes in, and a personalised offer comes out, with the business's logo already placed on the club's equipment. The jury can type any business and upload any logo.

The tool works in five steps. The club describes ten slots, each with a price, a status (free or taken), the current sponsor and its sector, as well as its needs and its fundraising goal. A guardrail then blocks alcohol, tobacco and gambling businesses before any call to the AI. The AI model chooses three offers among the free slots and writes the email. The code verifies the result: a taken slot is removed, prices come from the club's grid, and a business whose sector matches a current sponsor is flagged for human review. Finally, the logo is placed on photographs by perspective and lighting.

The behaviour is adapted to each case. A garage is offered the minibus and the entrance banner, and the offer is tied to the club's need to renew the minibus. A sports shop is offered the training bibs and the boards. An estate agency triggers a warning because a real estate group already sponsors the club. A business whose activity cannot be guessed from its name, such as "Chez Momo", is sent to a human.

4. How it is built

We apply the seven-layer model of the course. The default rule is to buy the model, build what makes the difference (orchestration and user experience), buy the commodity tools, and partner where someone else owns the access. Figure 3 gives the decision for each layer.

The prototype covers layers 3 to 5 and a light version of layer 7. Storage, distribution and public business directories belong to the roadmap and are not part of the demonstration. We chose the simplest agent shape that works, a fixed workflow with a single AI call, because it is cheaper, faster and easier to test than an agent loop.

The photographs are produced once with an image model, at a total cost of $0.47 for seven scenes. At run time the logo is placed by code, so images cost nothing and are instant. This also makes the demonstration reliable in front of a jury.

Measured on the prototype, one offer uses about 1560 input tokens and 780 output tokens with the small model, which costs about $0.0006. The writing takes 3.5 to 4.5 seconds, so the whole offer appears in four to eight seconds, above the three-second target of the course. Streaming the text is the first improvement.

5. Market

We size the market from the bottom up: the clubs that sign, multiplied by the price per club. The club, represented by its treasurer or president, is the customer who signs. We exclude small neighbourhood clubs, which make up 66% of clubs: their sponsoring is about €1,060 a year, which leaves under €100 of net gain, too little to pay for a tool.

Table 1. Market sizing, with annual prices of €180 for a mid-size club and €1,800 for a flagship club.
LevelClubsAnnual value
Total market in France51,150 mid-size, 4,950 flagship (56,100 in total)€18.1M
Reachable today (football and rugby)4,309 mid-size, 417 flagship (4,726 in total)€1.53M
Target in three years360 mid-size, 40 flagship€136,800

The target of 400 clubs in 36 months equals 11 new clubs a month, or 8.5% of the reachable clubs. We expect most of them to come through district and league partnerships that relay the tool, with direct calls as a complement. No agreement exists yet.

The sources are imperfect. The split of clubs by size comes from a study that reuses data from 2011 and 2012. The total number of clubs in France, about 165,000, comes from a weak source dated 2020. Club counts for football (about 12,000) and rugby (more than 1,900) come from the federations. These figures give orders of magnitude and should be cross-checked with the Ministry of Sports before any investor use.

6. Business model and price

The model is a software subscription per club, with two plans that follow the size of the club. For a club, the archetype is revenue uplift: the tool helps it present more adapted offers and sign more local sponsors. We count the net gain, after the cost of making the signs and the kit. We follow the course rule that a price should capture 10 to 30% of the value created, because cost-plus pricing would leave most of the value unclaimed.

The price of €15 stays below the €19 to €49 a month that clubs already pay for management software, so the tool is a light complement rather than a replacement. Two prices should not be confused: the €300 to €1,500 per season shown in the demonstration is what the club charges its sponsors, while the €15 and €150 a month are what we charge the club.

7. Competition and defensibility

We found several players around sports sponsorship in France. None of them, as far as we could verify from their own pages and press, prepares an offer per business from the club's free slots and shows the logo on the club's own equipment. We did not test these products ourselves.

Table 4. Players around sports sponsorship and the gap we address.
PlayerWhat it doesGap we address
All SponsoredScans clubs' social networks to measure brand visibility and brokers sponsoringNo offer per business, no mock-up of the club's own kit
LeedeelPlatform connecting brands with athletes, clubs and federationsA marketplace, not a tool that prepares the club's offer
Spencer.clubIntermediary for introductions, contracts and structuringA human service, not an instant tool
SPONSO+Participatory sponsoring by many small contributorsA different model, not packages for local businesses
Proposal and deck toolsTemplates, AI-assisted proposals, electronic signatureGeneric, with no club inventory or sector rule

What clubs hire today is the real competition: a volunteer's own pitch, free templates, or doing nothing. We apply the five forces of the course to this market. Suppliers, the model providers, hold medium power, and we reduce it by using two models. The threat of new entrants is high, because a prompt and a screen can be rebuilt in a weekend. Substitutes are strong, with free templates and general chat assistants. Buyers, the clubs, have low switching costs at first. Rivalry is medium for now.

Since the model cannot be defended, we rely on three moats. The first is data: which offers close, by sector and price, collected from the offers sent through the tool. The second is distribution through districts and leagues. The third is workflow: once the club keeps its inventory, sponsors and renewals in the tool, leaving costs time.

8. Financial plan

The plan assumes a linear ramp to 400 paying clubs over 36 months, a blended price of €28.5 a month, a blended cost to serve of €3.9 and fixed costs of €3,000 a month, which cover two small stipends and tools. The gross margin is 86%. The monthly result turns positive in month 11, after 122 clubs. The cumulative cash reaches its lowest point of €14,967 in month 10.

We ask for €35,000 to cover 18 months. This amount equals the cash low point of €14,967 plus six months of fixed costs (€18,000), rounded up. Within 18 months we aim for three pilot clubs with measured results, at least one agreement with a district or a league, and 122 paying clubs.

9. Responsible and scalable by design

Data protection. The prototype processes no personal data: it uses business names and a fictional club. In production the tool would handle club data and professional contacts. We would collect only what is needed, set a retention period, sign a data processing agreement with the model provider, and prefer hosting in the European Union. Prospecting emails to businesses must follow the rules on business-to-business marketing, which we still need to verify.

AI Act. We classify the tool as limited risk, since it is a text generator for sales offers, not a system that decides about people. The transparency duty applies, and the interface states under every email that the text was generated with the help of AI and must be reviewed before sending. The application dates of the regulation have evolved, so they must be checked on the official calendar before any commercial launch.

Fairness. The tool does not score or rank people. Its rules concern businesses: alcohol, tobacco and gambling are excluded because their advertising is restricted in sport, and a competitor of an existing sponsor is flagged. These rules still need to be confirmed with a federation.

Accountability. The model card would state the intended use (offers for local sponsors) and the out-of-scope uses (legal advice, regulated products). The datasheet would describe the club inventory fields and who updates them. The audit trail would record for each offer the input, the slots chosen, the model, the cost and the time. The prototype already displays cost and time for each offer.

Cost and latency at scale. At 400 clubs, about 7,800 offers a month cost about $4.3 with the small model, which is 0.04% of monthly revenue. With the large model the bill would be about $85, or 0.7%. The cost of the model is therefore not the main risk. The four to five seconds of writing time is the main technical point to improve.

10. Risks, assumptions and next steps

Our results rest on assumptions that we have not yet tested with clubs. We list the most important ones and how we will check them.

Table 6. Main assumptions and how to test them.
AssumptionValue usedHow we will test it
Sponsoring uplift at full use30%Three pilot clubs over one season, measured before and after
Year-1 adoption40%Usage in the pilots
Clubs pay for the tool€15 and €150 a monthTen calls to mid-size clubs
Districts relay the tool11 new clubs a monthTwo or three conversations with districts or leagues
Cost to serve€3 and €12 a monthReal hosting and support time in the pilots
Minibus slot price€800No public price found, to be confirmed with clubs

Other risks deserve attention. Competitors may add similar features, so distribution and data matter more than the interface. The use of a business's logo in a mock-up needs the business's consent, and the offer is only a proposal. The size of the market is small, which is why the amount requested is modest and the plan does not depend on a large raise.

The next steps for the next 30 days are to call ten mid-size clubs, to start three pilot clubs, and to meet two district or league contacts. The success criterion for a pilot is an increase of at least 15% in sponsoring, or two new sponsors per pilot club.
